about.title: Hemet Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: A work injury in Hemet rarely happens in a vacuum. Someone driving a delivery route along Florida Avenue, a crew working a build-out off Sanderson Avenue, a warehouse shift that ends with a back that won't straighten — each of these starts a process that most people have never had to navigate before. California's workers' compensation system is designed to cover medical care and partial wage replacement no matter who was at fault, and in most cases it is the only claim you can bring against your own employer. What many Hemet workers don't realize is that a second path can exist. If a subcontractor, a property owner, the maker of a faulty tool, or another driver on State Street contributed to what happened, that third party may be held responsible in a separate injury claim with its own two-year deadline. LawProactive is not a law firm. We are a free service that connects Riverside County workers with an independent attorney who can sort out which claims apply, so you can concentrate on healing rather than paperwork.

items.desc: You generally have 30 days to report a work injury to your employer, and third-party claims in California carry a two-year filing window. An early connection helps keep both on track.

items.desc: California law makes it illegal for an employer to punish you for reporting an injury or filing a claim. An independent attorney can explain your rights if you feel pressure at work.

items.question: I was hit while driving for my job on Florida Avenue in Hemet. Is that a workers' comp case or a car accident case?
items.answer: It can be both. If you were on the clock, workers' compensation typically covers your medical treatment and part of your lost wages regardless of who caused the crash. If the other driver was negligent, you may also have a separate third-party injury claim against them, which carries California's two-year deadline. Hemet recorded 273 injury collisions in 2025, and a fair number of those involved people simply getting through their workday.

items.question: My employer says I can't sue them. Is that true?
items.answer: In most situations, yes. California law makes workers' compensation the exclusive remedy against your employer, meaning you receive benefits without having to prove fault but generally cannot file a lawsuit against the company itself. That limit does not extend to outside parties such as a subcontractor, a property owner, or the maker of defective equipment. An attorney can review whether anyone other than your employer played a role.

items.question: I waited a few weeks to report my injury because I thought it would get better. Did I miss my chance?
items.answer: Not necessarily. California asks you to notify your employer within 30 days, so if you are still inside that window, report it in writing right away. Even if more time has passed, some claims can still move forward depending on the circumstances, and any third-party claim has its own two-year timeline. Reach out sooner rather than later so an independent attorney can look at the specific dates involved.
